original_question: (S. Harper, C. Donoven). The spread of a group G is the greatest nonnegative integer k such that for all nontrivial elements x1,..., xk ∈ G there exists y ∈ G such that ⟨x1, y⟩ = · · · = ⟨xk, y⟩ = G, or is ∞ in case there is no such maximum. Does there exist a group with spread equal to 1? Such a group must be infinite if it exists(T. C. Burness, R. M. Guralnick, S. Harper, Ann. Math., 193(2021), 619–687).
target_in_paper: Problem 21.38 in the section "New Problems (21st issue, 2026)": the existence of a group with spread equal to 1.
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper's official formulation. It correctly gives the definition of spread, asks exactly whether there exists a group with spread equal to 1, and includes the paper's accompanying note that any such group would have to be infinite.
missing_details: The paper states this specifically as Problem 21.38 in the section "New Problems (21st issue, 2026)".
The ambient scope is all groups; the problem does not assume finiteness, finite generation, simplicity, residual finiteness, or any other structural hypothesis.
To make the question fully stand-alone, it helps to name the invariant explicitly as s(G), the spread of G.
The quantifier over y depends on the whole tuple x_1, ..., x_k; this is not the stronger notion of uniform spread, where y is restricted to a fixed conjugacy class.
Since the paper immediately notes that any example must be infinite, the sharpest stand-alone restatement may say "infinite group" explicitly.
refined_question: Does there exist an infinite group G with spread s(G)=1, where s(G) is the greatest nonnegative integer k such that for every choice of nontrivial elements x_1, ..., x_k in G there exists an element y in G with the subgroup generated by x_i and y equal to G for every i=1, ..., k, and s(G)=∞ if no such maximum exists?
justification: The draft is essentially a restatement of Problem 21.38. On page 166, the paper defines the spread of a group exactly in these terms and then asks, without adding further hypotheses, whether there exists a group with spread equal to 1. The only paper-faithful sharpening is to introduce the notation s(G) and to fold in the accompanying comment that any such example must be infinite.
